evidence.explanation: Links the minor splicing defect in patient cells to altered expression of a disease-relevant gene subgroup.

evidence.snippet: Our findings demonstrate a crucial role of the minor spliceosome component U4atac snRNA in early human development and postnatal survival.
evidence.explanation: Connects the molecular lesion to the developmental and survival phenotype.

evidence.snippet: mRNA splicing (U4atac), and centrosome function (CEP152, PCNT, and CPAP)
evidence.explanation: Places U4atac in the mRNA-splicing class of microcephalic primordial dwarfism genes, distinct from the centrosomal class that includes PCNT (MOPD II).

steps/5.description: Because minor introns are concentrated in genes governing DNA replication and repair, transcription, RNA processing, and translation, minor splicing failure compromises the cell populations most dependent on those processes during embryogenesis — cortical neural progenitors and growth plate chondrocytes above all. The result is the combined brain-and-bone phenotype: severe microcephaly with structural cortical malformation and a generalized skeletal dysplasia, on a background of extreme prenatal growth restriction.

evidence.snippet: The main features of MOPD I patients are extreme intrauterine growth retardation, abnormalities in multiple organs, and death in infancy or early childhood
evidence.explanation: States extreme IUGR as a main feature of MOPD I.

evidence.snippet: Findings present in all affected individuals include growth restriction, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, and cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes growth restriction as universal across the RNU4ATAC spectrum, supporting the OBLIGATE frequency band.

steps/6.description: Profound prenatal-onset growth failure is a defining feature, present in all affected individuals and detectable antenatally.

evidence.snippet: This syndrome is characterized by short stature, skeletal anomalies, severe microcephaly with brain malformations and facial dysmorphism, and is caused by mutations in RNU4ATAC.
evidence.explanation: Lists short stature among the defining features of TALS.

evidence.snippet: These rare developmental disorders, whose physiopathological mechanisms remain unsolved, associate ante- and post-natal growth retardation, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, intellectual disability, retinal dystrophy, and immunodeficiency.
evidence.explanation: Documents both antenatal and postnatal growth retardation across the RNU4ATAC disorders.

steps/7.description: Growth restriction continues after birth, producing severe short stature without catch-up growth.

evidence.snippet: Findings present in all affected individuals include growth restriction, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, and cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes microcephaly as universal, supporting the OBLIGATE frequency band.

evidence.snippet: This syndrome is characterized by short stature, skeletal anomalies, severe microcephaly with brain malformations and facial dysmorphism, and is caused by mutations in RNU4ATAC.
evidence.explanation: Specifies severe microcephaly with brain malformations.

steps/8.description: Severe congenital microcephaly is universal and, unlike in MOPD II, is accompanied by structural brain malformation and profound cognitive impairment.

evidence.snippet: We identified four point mutations in the U4atac snRNA component of the minor spliceosome in patients with brain and bone malformations and unexplained postnatal death
evidence.explanation: Documents brain malformation as a presenting feature of the TALS cohort.

evidence.snippet: Less common but variable findings include brain anomalies, seizures, strokes, immunodeficiency, and cardiac anomalies, as well as ophthalmologic, skin, renal, gastrointestinal, hearing, and endocrine involvement.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes brain anomalies as a variable finding across the whole RNU4ATAC spectrum, which includes milder Roifman and Lowry-Wood presentations; support is recorded as PARTIAL because the spectrum-wide statement understates the frequency at the MOPD I end.

steps/9.description: Brain malformations — including agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a simplified gyral pattern or lissencephaly-like cortex, and cerebellar vermis hypoplasia — are a core discriminating feature of MOPD I relative to MOPD II, where the brain is small but structurally unremarkable. This entry curates the brain-malformation claim at the level the cited abstracts support (malformation present); the specific radiological subtypes named in the description are drawn from the wider literature and are not individually snippet-verified here.

evidence.snippet: The patients showed the classical phenotype and demonstrated in addition variable degrees of gyration abnormalities and malformations of the callosal body with an interhemispheric cyst.
evidence.explanation: Documents gyration abnormalities in five molecularly confirmed MOPD I patients.

evidence.snippet: This confirms that cortical malformations should be considered cardinal manifestations of MOPD I.
evidence.explanation: Supports treating cortical malformation as a core rather than incidental feature.

steps/10.description: Gyration abnormalities are seen alongside the microcephaly. The authors of the largest RNU4ATAC-confirmed series argue that cortical malformations should be regarded as cardinal rather than incidental manifestations of MOPD I.

evidence.snippet: microcephaly with abnormal gyral pattern and partial agenesis of corpus callosum
evidence.explanation: Documents partial callosal agenesis in RNU4ATAC-confirmed sibs.

evidence.snippet: malformations of the callosal body with an interhemispheric cyst
evidence.explanation: Independent series documenting callosal malformation.

steps/11.description: Malformations of the corpus callosum, including partial agenesis and callosal malformation with an interhemispheric cyst, are part of the structural brain phenotype.

evidence.snippet: One patient also showed underdevelopment of the cerebellar vermis.
evidence.explanation: One of five patients, supporting the OCCASIONAL frequency band.

steps/12.description: Underdevelopment of the cerebellar vermis has been documented in the RNU4ATAC-confirmed series, and is one of the features that overlaps the Joubert-like presentations at the ciliary end of the spectrum.

evidence.snippet: The sibs had yellowish-gray hair, fair skin, and deficient retinal pigmentation.
evidence.explanation: Direct description of the hair and skin pigmentary phenotype in RNU4ATAC-confirmed sibs.

evidence.snippet: The present study showed lack of retinal pigmentation in three patients of whom two had an unusually fair complexion of hair and skin.
evidence.explanation: Independent series confirming the hair pigmentary phenotype in two of five RNU4ATAC-confirmed patients. Supports the association only; no frequency band is asserted from this within-series proportion.

steps/13.description:
Pigmentary abnormality of the hair — yellowish-gray hair and an unusually fair complexion — has been reported in RNU4ATAC-confirmed MOPD I, with skin biopsy showing abnormal melanin function despite normal oculocutaneous albinism genes. Note that this is a pigmentary rather than a structural hair abnormality; see the entry notes on why sparse/absent hair is not curated here. The skin and fundus arms of the same finding are curated separately below, because HP:0011358 is hair-specific by definition.
frequency is intentionally omitted: the only denominators available are two small series from a single group, and the disease-level rate is unknown. See the entry notes.

evidence.snippet: The sibs had yellowish-gray hair, fair skin, and deficient retinal pigmentation.
evidence.explanation: Attests fair skin in RNU4ATAC-confirmed sibs.

evidence.snippet: Skin biopsy showed abnormal melanin function but OCA genes were normal.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the skin hypopigmentation reflects a melanin-function defect distinct from classical oculocutaneous albinism.

evidence.snippet: The present study showed lack of retinal pigmentation in three patients of whom two had an unusually fair complexion of hair and skin.
evidence.explanation: Independent series attesting fair skin complexion in two of five RNU4ATAC-confirmed patients. Supports the association only; no frequency band is asserted from this within-series proportion.

steps/14.description:
The skin arm of the RNU4ATAC-associated pigmentary phenotype: fair skin and an unusually fair complexion, with skin biopsy showing abnormal melanin function despite normal oculocutaneous albinism genes. Curated as a separate phenotype from the hair finding because HP:0011358 is hair-specific, so the skin involvement attested by the same two sentences would otherwise be unbound and unqueryable.
frequency is intentionally omitted for the same reason as the hair arm.

evidence.snippet: The sibs had yellowish-gray hair, fair skin, and deficient retinal pigmentation.
evidence.explanation: Attests deficient retinal pigmentation alongside the hair and skin arms in RNU4ATAC-confirmed sibs.

evidence.snippet: The present study showed lack of retinal pigmentation in three patients of whom two had an unusually fair complexion of hair and skin.
evidence.explanation: Independent series attesting lack of retinal pigmentation in three of five RNU4ATAC-confirmed patients. Supports the association only; no frequency band is asserted from this within-series proportion.

steps/15.description:
The retinal arm of the RNU4ATAC-associated pigmentary triad: deficient or absent retinal pigmentation, reported alongside the hair and skin findings in the same patients. This is distinct from the Retinal Dystrophy entry below, which is a degenerative claim drawn from the broader RNU4ATAC spectrum; this is a developmental pigmentary deficit described in MOPD I specifically. HP:0007894 is defined as reduced fundus pigmentation evaluated in the context of skin and hair color, which is exactly how both sources report it.
frequency is intentionally omitted for the same reason as the hair and skin arms.

evidence.snippet: Findings present in all affected individuals include growth restriction, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, and cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes cognitive impairment as universal, supporting the OBLIGATE frequency band.

evidence.snippet: These rare developmental disorders, whose physiopathological mechanisms remain unsolved, associate ante- and post-natal growth retardation, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, intellectual disability, retinal dystrophy, and immunodeficiency.
evidence.explanation: Independent listing of intellectual disability among the core features.

steps/16.description: Cognitive impairment is present in all affected individuals across the RNU4ATAC spectrum and is profound at the MOPD I end. This is one of the sharpest discriminators from MOPD II, where intelligence is near-normal.

evidence.snippet: Less common but variable findings include brain anomalies, seizures, strokes, immunodeficiency, and cardiac anomalies, as well as ophthalmologic, skin, renal, gastrointestinal, hearing, and endocrine involvement.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists seizures among the less common, variable findings, supporting the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/17.description: Seizures occur as a variable finding across the RNU4ATAC spectrum and are a common feature at the severe MOPD I end.

evidence.snippet: For those with MOPDI, minimize medically stressful situations as much as possible, including stress during anesthesia, due to energy-related strokes.
evidence.explanation: Documents strokes in MOPD I specifically and their precipitation by physiologic stress.

evidence.snippet: particularly brain MRI for detection of stroke in children with MOPDI with neurologic deterioration
evidence.explanation: Surveillance recommendation confirming stroke as a recognized MOPD I complication.

steps/18.description: Strokes occur in MOPD I and are described by GeneReviews as energy-related, prompting the specific management recommendations to minimize medically stressful situations including anesthesia and to obtain brain MRI when a child with MOPD I shows neurologic deterioration.

evidence.snippet: Findings present in all affected individuals include growth restriction, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, and cognitive impairment.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes skeletal dysplasia as universal, supporting the OBLIGATE frequency band.

evidence.snippet: This syndrome is characterized by short stature, skeletal anomalies, severe microcephaly with brain malformations and facial dysmorphism, and is caused by mutations in RNU4ATAC.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of skeletal anomalies as a defining feature.

steps/19.description: A generalized skeletal dysplasia is universal across the RNU4ATAC spectrum. In MOPD I it includes short, bowed long bones with abnormal metaphyses and delayed epiphyseal maturation, with vertebral and pelvic anomalies; the radiographic pattern was the historical basis for separating MOPD I from MOPD III before both were shown to be RNU4ATAC-related.

evidence.snippet: This syndrome is characterized by short stature, skeletal anomalies, severe microcephaly with brain malformations and facial dysmorphism, and is caused by mutations in RNU4ATAC.
evidence.explanation: Lists facial dysmorphism among the defining features.

evidence.snippet: We provide antenatal descriptions of this rare syndrome including unusual features found in two twin foetuses with compound heterozygosity for two rare mutations who presented with mild intrauterine growth retardation and atypical dysmorphic facial features.
evidence.explanation: Documents dysmorphic facial features, including atypical variants, in antenatally ascertained cases.

steps/20.description: A characteristic facial gestalt accompanies the microcephaly and is part of the antenatal and postnatal diagnostic picture.

evidence.snippet: Less common but variable findings include brain anomalies, seizures, strokes, immunodeficiency, and cardiac anomalies, as well as ophthalmologic, skin, renal, gastrointestinal, hearing, and endocrine involvement.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists immunodeficiency among the variable findings across the spectrum.

evidence.snippet: These rare developmental disorders, whose physiopathological mechanisms remain unsolved, associate ante- and post-natal growth retardation, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, intellectual disability, retinal dystrophy, and immunodeficiency.
evidence.explanation: Independent listing of immunodeficiency among the RNU4ATAC disorder features.

steps/21.description: Immunodeficiency (hypogammaglobulinemia, lymphopenia) is a variable feature across the RNU4ATAC spectrum; it is the defining feature at the Roifman end but also occurs in MOPD I, where recognition matters because infection is a major cause of death and because live vaccines require prior immunologic evaluation.

evidence.snippet: These rare developmental disorders, whose physiopathological mechanisms remain unsolved, associate ante- and post-natal growth retardation, microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, intellectual disability, retinal dystrophy, and immunodeficiency.
evidence.explanation: Lists retinal dystrophy among the shared features of TALS, Roifman, and Lowry-Wood syndromes.

steps/22.description: Retinal dystrophy is part of the RNU4ATAC phenotypic spectrum, most prominent in Roifman and Lowry-Wood syndromes but recognized as part of the ophthalmologic involvement documented across the spectrum.

edges/5.description: Photoreceptor outer segments are modified primary cilia, so ciliary dysfunction is the direct route to the retinal phenotype.

edges/6.description: Grouped with the other hypopigmentation findings, which are characteristic of MOPD I; no mechanism has been established, and the ciliary attribution is provisional.

edges/7.description: As for hair hypopigmentation: characteristic but mechanistically unexplained.

edges/8.description: As for the other hypopigmentation findings, and additionally part of the ocular involvement.

edges/9.description: Reported in this disorder and grouped provisionally with the vascular arm. A cerebrovascular mechanism is established for the related PCNT disorder MOPD II but not for RNU4ATAC, so this edge records the association rather than a demonstrated route.

edges/10.description: Prenatal arm of the proliferation deficit across tissues.

edges/11.description: Postnatal arm of the same deficit; there is no catch-up phase.

edges/12.description: Neural progenitor populations are among the most proliferation-dependent, which is why the brain deficit is disproportionate.

edges/13.description: Failure of progenitor expansion during corticogenesis.

edges/14.description: Consequence of reduced cortical neuron output and disturbed progenitor dynamics.

edges/15.description: Commissural axon guidance depends on the cell populations this node describes; grouped with the other structural brain findings.

edges/16.description: Cerebellar granule progenitors are highly proliferative; grouped with the other structural brain findings.

edges/17.description: Functional consequence of the structural brain deficits.

edges/18.description: Grouped with the cortical malformations, which are the usual substrate for the epilepsy in this disorder.

edges/19.description: Growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation shares the same deficit, giving the osteodysplastic component of the name.

edges/20.description: Craniofacial consequence of impaired progenitor proliferation; no specific route is established.

edges/21.description: Lymphoid development is minor-intron sensitive; in the milder RNU4ATAC phenotypes this arm dominates, and it is present here too.

evidence.snippet: Functional assays showed that mutations (30G>A, 51G>A, 55G>A, and 111G>A) associated with MOPD I cause defective U12-dependent splicing.
evidence.explanation: Names the founding MOPD I variant set and demonstrates their functional consequence.

evidence.snippet: Strikingly, all six of the Roifman Syndrome cases have one variant that overlaps MOPD1-implicated structural elements, while the other variant overlaps a highly conserved structural element not previously implicated in disease.
evidence.explanation: Supports allele combination as the determinant of position on the RNU4ATAC phenotypic spectrum.

genes/0.notes: RNU4ATAC (2q14.2) is a single-copy, non-protein-coding gene encoding the U4atac small nuclear RNA of the minor spliceosome. All reported pathogenic variants are single-nucleotide substitutions clustering in the 5' stem-loop and Stem II structural domains. n.51G>A is an Old Order Amish founder allele and the most frequently reported pathogenic variant. Allele combination is the principal determinant of where an individual falls on the RNU4ATAC spectrum: variants that overlap MOPD I-implicated structural elements paired with a milder second allele shift the phenotype toward Roifman or Lowry-Wood syndrome. Because complete U4atac loss is expected to be lethal, disease alleles are hypomorphic.

evidence.snippet: This ideally involves multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields, including orthopedists to monitor the associated skeletal dysplasia and immunologists to manage antibiotic treatment of infections and use of immunoglobulin replacement therapy as indicated to avoid life-threatening infections.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews treatment-of-manifestations statement.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary, aimed at quality of life, function, and complication reduction — notably orthopedic monitoring of the skeletal dysplasia and immunologic management, including immunoglobulin replacement where indicated, to avoid life-threatening infections.

evidence.snippet: Perform immunologic evaluation prior to administration of live vaccines.
evidence.explanation: Records the GeneReviews agents/circumstances-to-avoid instruction.

treatments/1.description: Because immunodeficiency occurs across the RNU4ATAC spectrum, GeneReviews directs that immunologic evaluation be performed before any live vaccine is administered. This is a safety precaution rather than a therapy.

evidence.snippet: For those with MOPDI, minimize medically stressful situations as much as possible, including stress during anesthesia, due to energy-related strokes.
evidence.explanation: Records the MOPD I-specific GeneReviews agents-to-avoid warning verbatim.

treatments/2.description: For individuals with MOPD I specifically, medically stressful situations — including anesthesia — should be minimized because of the risk of energy-related strokes. This is a disease-specific perioperative safety warning.

evidence.snippet: Once the RNU4ATAC pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic-counseling statement.

treatments/3.description: Counseling for autosomal recessive recurrence risk, with carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing available once the familial RNU4ATAC variants are known. Counseling should include the observation that siblings with identical genotypes can differ clinically.

open_questions/0.rationale: The zebrafish work is the strongest in vivo support for the ciliary arm of RNU4ATAC disease, but its design is dose-titration of an essential gene rather than modeling of a specific patient allele, and the human phenotypes it reproduces best (pronephric cysts, otolith defects, body-axis curvature) are not the phenotypes that dominate human MOPD I (microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, growth restriction). Whether the ciliary mechanism carries the same weight in human brain and skeletal development as it does in the fish phenotypes is therefore an open translational question, not a settled one.

open_questions/1.rationale: The proximal molecular defect is established with unusual clarity, but the step from genome-wide minor-intron mis-splicing to the specific brain-and-bone phenotype is inferred from the functional enrichment of minor-intron-containing genes rather than demonstrated for named effectors. Transcriptomic work moreover shows that mRNA levels are mostly unchanged, so a simple dosage model of the intervening step is not supported.

evidence.snippet:
Among men 
with independent TGCT risk factors such as cryptorchidism
evidence.explanation: Identifies cryptorchidism as an established independent risk factor for TGCT.

evidence.snippet: By meta-analysis of data from the six qualifying studies, the summary odds ratio estimate of the in utero DES-testicular cancer association was 2.98 (95% confidence interval = 1.15 to 7.67).
evidence.explanation: Supports the diethylstilbestrol half of this exposure with a pooled odds ratio of about three. Because DES use ceased in 1971, the authors note this is likely the most complete estimate that will ever be made.

evidence.snippet: Prenatal exposure to OCPs and PCBs, quantified by concentrations in maternal pregnancy serum, was not associated with later risk of TGCC.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the organochlorine and PCB half as previously stated. A nested case-control study measured seven organochlorine pesticides and thirteen PCB congeners directly in maternal pregnancy serum, rather than relying on recall or occupational proxies, and found no association. Recorded rather than dropped, so the stronger claim is not reintroduced.

evidence.snippet:
Pediatric germ cell tumors represent a rare but biologically diverse group of 
neoplasms arising from pluripotent primordial germ cells.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the pluripotent primordial germ cell origin shared by germ cell tumors including mixed histologies.

steps/2.description: Mixed germ cell tumors originate from primordial germ cells (PGCs) / gonocytes that fail to differentiate normally during fetal development and persist in a pluripotent state. In post-pubertal-type tumors this gives rise to germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS), the common precursor lesion from which the invasive tumor and all of its histologic components derive.

evidence.snippet:
Despite high aneuploidy and a paucity of somatic mutations, several 
genomic and transcriptomic assays have identified a few significantly mutated 
somatic genes, primarily KIT and K-RAS.
evidence.explanation: Describes the aneuploid genome (of which i(12p) is the hallmark) with few recurrent somatic mutations, primarily KIT and K-RAS, in TGCTs.

steps/3.description: Isochromosome 12p [i(12p)] is the hallmark cytogenetic abnormality of invasive post-pubertal-type germ cell tumors, present in the large majority of cases, and marks the transition from in situ GCNIS to invasive disease. The 12p amplicon harbors candidate drivers including KRAS and the pluripotency and germ-cell genes that sustain the transformed precursor; its detection by FISH distinguishes post-pubertal from pre-pubertal type tumors.

evidence.snippet:
several 
genomic and transcriptomic assays have identified a few significantly mutated 
somatic genes, primarily KIT and K-RAS.
evidence.explanation: Identifies KIT and K-RAS / the RAS-MAPK pathway as the principal recurrent somatic drivers in germ cell tumors.

steps/4.description: KIT and K-RAS are the most significantly mutated somatic genes in germ cell tumors. KIT (a stem-cell growth factor receptor controlling germ cell survival, proliferation, and migration) is mutated in 18-25% of cases, chiefly in seminomatous components, and KRAS shows copy-number gain in the majority of tumors with activating mutations in roughly a quarter. The resulting KIT-RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade is constitutively activated and drives proliferation of the transformed precursor.

evidence.snippet:
These 
updates enhance diagnostic accuracy and provide a framework for 
understanding age-dependent differences in tumor biology and behavior.
evidence.explanation: The 2022 WHO organ-independent classification frames the histologic subtypes whose coexistence defines mixed germ cell tumor.

steps/5.description: The defining event of a mixed germ cell tumor is simultaneous (divergent) differentiation of the pluripotent transformed precursor along multiple embryonic and extraembryonic lineages, producing two or more coexisting histologic components: embryonal carcinoma (pluripotent), yolk sac tumor (extraembryonic endoderm), choriocarcinoma (trophoblast), teratoma (somatic tri-lineage), and seminoma/dysgerminoma (gonocytic). The specific combination determines the serum marker profile and biologic behavior.

evidence.snippet:
The initial 
phase of TGCT diagnosis is performed by detecting in the blood the presence of 
three proteins, i.e., alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and 
human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).
evidence.explanation: Establishes AFP (with LDH and hCG) as a serum diagnostic marker of germ cell tumors; AFP reflects the yolk sac component.

steps/6.description: The yolk sac tumor component recapitulates primitive (extraembryonic) endoderm and secretes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), producing elevated serum AFP. AFP is therefore elevated when a yolk sac (or embryonal carcinoma) component is present but never in pure seminoma or pure choriocarcinoma.

evidence.snippet:
hCG can be elevated in 
both seminomas and non-seminomas, reducing its ability to differentiate between 
tumor types.
evidence.explanation: Describes beta-hCG as a germ cell tumor marker secreted across tumor types, maximally by the choriocarcinoma (trophoblastic) component.

steps/7.description: The choriocarcinoma component recapitulates trophoblast and contains syncytiotrophoblasts that secrete beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG). Markedly elevated beta-hCG (often >50,000 IU/L) accompanies a choriocarcinoma component, and hCG can also be mildly elevated by syncytiotrophoblasts in other components.

evidence.snippet:
Non-seminoma PMGCTs have the shortest 
5-year overall survival and the poorest prognosis among all of the germ cell 
tumor presentations
evidence.explanation: Documents the aggressive behavior and poor prognosis of non-seminomatous (including mixed) germ cell tumors, here in the mediastinal setting.

steps/8.description: Mixed germ cell tumors are non-seminomatous tumors that generally behave more aggressively than pure seminoma, with higher rates of lymphovascular invasion and a propensity for visceral metastasis to lungs and liver, especially when choriocarcinoma or embryonal carcinoma components predominate. The growing mass produces the presenting gonadal or extragonadal tumor.

evidence.snippet:
Most of patients have a good 
prognosis, often even in the presence of metastatic disease; however, in almost 
15% of cases, tumor relapse and platinum resistance are the main challenges.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the good prognosis from platinum sensitivity and the ~15% platinum-resistant fraction that drives treatment failure.

steps/9.description: Germ cell tumors are exquisitely sensitive to cisplatin-based chemotherapy because of a hypersensitive apoptotic response and limited DNA-damage repair capacity, allowing cure even in widely metastatic disease. Approximately 15% of patients nonetheless develop platinum-refractory disease through mechanisms including increased DNA methylation/epigenetic reprogramming, enhanced DNA repair, and anti-apoptotic signaling, which is the principal cause of germ cell tumor mortality.

evidence.snippet:
Testicular GCTs (TGCTs) are the 
most common cancers in 15- to 39-year-old men, and ovarian GCTs (OvGCTs) are the 
leading gynecologic malignancies in women younger than 25 years.
evidence.explanation: Documents the gonadal presentation of germ cell tumors in the characteristic age groups.

steps/10.description: Mixed germ cell tumors present as a mass at gonadal (painless testicular mass; large fast-growing ovarian mass with abdominal pain) or extragonadal midline sites (anterior mediastinum, retroperitoneum, CNS).

steps/11.description: Gynecomastia may occur due to beta-hCG production (especially by a choriocarcinoma component), which stimulates estrogen production.

edges/0.description: GCNIS progresses to invasive germ cell tumor upon gain of chromosome 12p, typically as isochromosome 12p.

edges/1.description: Amplification of KRAS on 12p together with activating KIT and RAS mutations drives constitutive proliferative signaling.

edges/2.description: The proliferating pluripotent precursor differentiates simultaneously along multiple lineages, generating the mixed histologic components.

edges/3.description: A yolk sac component differentiates and secretes alpha-fetoprotein.

edges/4.description: A choriocarcinoma component differentiates and its syncytiotrophoblasts secrete beta-hCG.

edges/5.description: The combined components form an invasive, often rapidly growing tumor mass with metastatic potential.

edges/6.description: beta-hCG stimulates estrogen production, which can cause gynecomastia.

edges/7.description: Invasive growth presents as a testicular, ovarian, mediastinal, or other extragonadal mass.

edges/8.description: Platinum resistance permits persistence/relapse of the tumor mass.

evidence.snippet: Among men with independent TGCT risk factors such as cryptorchidism
evidence.explanation: Names cryptorchidism among the independent risk factors for this tumour, in a sentence whose subject is how a polygenic risk score might guide screening in men who have them.

edges/9.description: Pointed at the germ-cell maldifferentiation node because the testicular dysgenesis model treats undescended testis and the tumour as shared consequences of a disturbed fetal gonadal programme, which is what that node holds. Graded partial for a reason worth stating: the only sentence available names cryptorchidism as an independent risk factor in a subordinate clause of a sentence that is really about polygenic risk scores guiding screening. It confirms the risk factor in passing and quantifies nothing about it.

evidence.snippet: Because evidence suggests that TGCT is initiated in very early life
evidence.explanation: The premise that makes this edge point at the fetal germ-cell node rather than at a later step. Indirect because it is the authors' framing of prior evidence, not a result of this study.

edges/10.description: Pointed at the germ-cell maldifferentiation node for the same reason as cryptorchidism: the testicular dysgenesis model holds that an endocrine disturbance of the fetal gonadal programme is what these exposures act on. The intermediates are unknown, and the edge is agent-specific rather than class-wide: the diethylstilbestrol evidence is what carries it, while the strongest prenatal measurement of organochlorine pesticides and PCBs found no association with later tumour risk.

evidence.snippet: Despite high aneuploidy and a paucity of somatic mutations
evidence.explanation: Describes the highly aneuploid genome of germ cell tumors, of which i(12p) is the defining cytogenetic feature.

evidence.snippet: primarily KIT and K-RAS.
evidence.explanation: Identifies KIT as one of the two principal recurrent somatic drivers in germ cell tumors.

evidence.snippet: primarily KIT and K-RAS.
evidence.explanation: Identifies K-RAS as one of the two principal recurrent somatic drivers in germ cell tumors.

treatments/0.description: Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the primary diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for a suspected testicular germ cell tumor, providing tissue for histologic diagnosis and pathologic staging.

treatments/1.description: For ovarian mixed germ cell tumors in young patients, fertility-sparing surgery (unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with preservation of the contralateral ovary and uterus) is prioritized.

evidence.snippet:
Excellent 
outcomes, even in widely metastatic disease using cisplatin-based chemotherapy, 
can be achieved since Einhorn and Donohue's landmark 1977 study in TGCT.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the high cure rate of cisplatin-based chemotherapy in metastatic germ cell tumor.

treatments/2.description: Bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin (BEP) is the standard first-line chemotherapy for metastatic germ cell tumor; germ cell tumors are exquisitely sensitive to cisplatin-based chemotherapy, achieving cure even in widely metastatic disease. Three cycles for good-risk and four cycles for intermediate/poor-risk disease.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: BEP exploits the hypersensitive apoptotic response and limited DNA-repair capacity of germ cell tumor cells; platinum resistance is the principal cause of treatment failure.

treatments/3.description: Alternative cisplatin-based regimens: EP (etoposide, cisplatin) and VIP (etoposide, ifosfamide, cisplatin) when bleomycin is contraindicated, and TIP (paclitaxel, ifosfamide, cisplatin) as second-line therapy for relapsed disease.

treatments/4.description: Resection of residual masses after chemotherapy (e.g., retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) is crucial for non-seminomatous germ cell tumors because residual masses may contain viable tumor or chemoresistant teratoma.

treatments/5.description: Sperm banking before treatment is recommended for fertility preservation in patients undergoing orchiectomy and gonadotoxic chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: NF1-null SLCs formed bona fide neurofibromas with high levels of SOX10 expression
evidence.explanation: Isogenic patient-derived hiPSC Schwannian-lineage cells form neurofibromas only when NF1 is biallelically inactivated (NF1-null), establishing that complete NF1 loss in the Schwann cell lineage is required for tumor formation.

steps/1.description: Neurofibroma initiation requires loss of both NF1 alleles in a Schwann cell lineage progenitor. In NF1 patients, one germline loss-of-function NF1 variant is inherited and a somatic second hit (loss of heterozygosity) inactivates the remaining wild-type allele, following the classic Knudson two-hit model. Sporadic solitary neurofibromas arise from two somatic NF1 hits in the absence of a germline variant.

evidence.snippet: The NF1 gene encodes neurofibromin, a large protein with RAS GTP-ase activating (RAS-GAP) activity, and loss of NF1 results in increased RAS signaling.
evidence.explanation: Directly states that NF1 loss removes the RAS-GAP activity of neurofibromin and increases RAS signaling.

steps/2.description: Neurofibromin is a RAS-GTPase-activating protein (RAS-GAP) that normally converts active RAS-GTP to inactive RAS-GDP. Its loss leaves RAS in the active GTP-bound state, producing constitutive RAS signal transduction that feeds the downstream RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK) and PI3K-AKT-mTOR effector cascades.

evidence.snippet: in addition to regulating MAPK-mediated cell growth
evidence.explanation: Identifies MAPK-mediated cell growth as a core consequence of NF1 loss in the Schwann cell lineage neurofibroma model.

steps/3.description: Sustained RAS-GTP signaling constitutively activates the RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK) cascade, the dominant proliferative signal in NF1-deficient Schwann cells and the molecular target of MEK1/2 inhibitors such as selumetinib.

evidence.snippet: NF1 loss impaired Schwann cell differentiation by inducing a persistent stem-like state to expand the pool of progenitors required to initiate tumor formation
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the differentiation block and progenitor-pool expansion mechanism upstream of tumor initiation.

steps/4.description: Beyond its effect on RAS-MAPK growth signaling, NF1 loss impairs Schwann cell differentiation, inducing a persistent stem-like state that expands the pool of SOX10+ progenitors competent to initiate a neurofibroma.

evidence.snippet: both Nf1 alleles were inactivated in mouse Sox10+ cells, leading to classic nodular cutaneous and plexiform neurofibroma formation that completely recapitulated their human counterparts
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates in a genetically engineered mouse model that biallelic Nf1 loss in Sox10+ Schwann lineage cells drives proliferation into cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas matching human tumors.

steps/5.description: Proliferation of NF1-null Schwann cells and SOX10+ progenitor-like cells generates the neoplastic compartment of the neurofibroma. Inactivation of both Nf1 alleles in Sox10+ cells is sufficient to generate classic nodular cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas in vivo.

evidence.snippet: showed dramatic expansion of immune and stromal cell populations; in corresponding human PNs, the immune and stromal cells comprised 90% of cells
evidence.explanation: Single-cell RNA sequencing shows that immune and stromal cells, not Schwann cells, make up the bulk (~90%) of human plexiform neurofibroma cellularity.

steps/6.description: Long after Nf1 loss, neurofibromas recruit and reprogram a complex microenvironment: in human plexiform neurofibromas immune and stromal cells comprise roughly 90% of the tumor, with monocyte recruitment, aberrant macrophage differentiation, fibroblast-driven collagen deposition, and deregulated cell-cell communication (e.g., MIF-CD74/NF-kB). This microenvironment supports tumor growth and immunosuppression and contributes to mass effect, pain, and disfigurement.

evidence.snippet: Plexiform neurofibroma (PN) and atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of unknown biological potential (ANNUBP) are novel concepts of MPNST precancerous lesions, which revealed sequential mutations in MPNST development.
evidence.explanation: Establishes plexiform neurofibroma and ANNUBP as sequential precursor lesions in the neurofibroma-to-MPNST malignant progression pathway.

steps/7.description: Plexiform neurofibromas are precursor lesions for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor. Transformation follows a stepwise molecular cascade: on the background of biallelic NF1 loss, inactivation of CDKN2A/B yields an atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biological potential (ANNUBP), and subsequent disruption of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2; SUZ12/EED) with loss of H3K27me3 drives progression to high-grade MPNST.

evidence.snippet: affected patients develop Schwann cell lineage peripheral nerve sheath tumors (neurofibromas)
evidence.explanation: Defines neurofibromas as Schwann cell lineage peripheral nerve sheath tumors, the core phenotype of this entry.

steps/8.description: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the Schwann cell lineage, presenting most commonly as cutaneous, subcutaneous, or spinal lesions.

evidence.snippet: Plexiform neurofibroma (PN) and atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of unknown biological potential (ANNUBP) are novel concepts of MPNST precancerous lesions
evidence.explanation: Supports the plexiform neurofibroma subtype and its precursor role for malignant transformation.

steps/9.description: Neurofibroma arising along multiple fascicles of large nerves and plexuses, frequently congenital, and a precursor to MPNST.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent neurofibroma-related symptoms were disfigurement (44 patients), motor dysfunction (33), and pain (26).
evidence.explanation: In the SPRINT trial cohort of symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas, pain was among the most frequent neurofibroma-related symptoms.

steps/10.description: Neurofibroma-related pain is a frequent and clinically significant symptom, particularly with plexiform neurofibromas, and is a primary driver of treatment.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent neurofibroma-related symptoms were disfigurement (44 patients), motor dysfunction (33), and pain (26).
evidence.explanation: In the SPRINT trial, motor dysfunction was among the most frequent plexiform-neurofibroma complications (33 of 50 patients).

steps/11.description: Motor dysfunction (weakness and reduced strength/range of motion) from tumor mass effect and nerve involvement is a frequent plexiform neurofibroma complication; SPRINT measured strength improvement with selumetinib.

evidence.snippet: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is an aggressive soft tissue sarcoma with limited therapeutic options and a poor prognosis.
evidence.explanation: Characterizes MPNST, the malignant tumor that plexiform neurofibromas can transform into.

steps/12.description: Malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma to an aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma (neurofibrosarcoma / MPNST).

edges/1.description: Loss of neurofibromin removes its RAS-GTPase-activating function, de-repressing RAS in the neoplastic Schwann cell lineage.

evidence.snippet: in addition to regulating MAPK-mediated cell growth, NF1 loss also altered Schwann cell differentiation to promote neurofibroma development
evidence.explanation: Directly supports a differentiation-altering effect of NF1 loss distinct from its MAPK growth effect.

edges/2.description: NF1 loss alters Schwann cell differentiation in addition to its effect on RAS-driven growth.

edges/3.description: Active RAS-GTP drives the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, the principal proliferative output downstream of NF1 loss and the target of MEK inhibitor therapy.

edges/4.description: MAPK-driven growth signaling promotes proliferation of the neoplastic Schwann cell lineage.

edges/5.description: The expanded stem-like progenitor pool provides the cells of origin that proliferate to form the tumor.

edges/6.description: The expanding NF1-null Schwann cell population recruits and reprograms immune and stromal cells, which come to dominate the tumor mass.

edges/7.description: Sustained proliferation of the neoplastic Schwann cell lineage forms the localized (cutaneous, subcutaneous, spinal) neurofibroma.

edges/8.description: When initiated in Schwann lineage cells along large nerves and plexuses, the proliferating tumor forms a plexiform neurofibroma.

edges/9.description: A subset of plexiform neurofibromas accumulate additional somatic lesions and progress along the pathway to malignant transformation.

edges/10.description: Tumor mass, nerve involvement, and the inflammatory microenvironment contribute to neurofibroma-associated pain.

edges/11.description: Tumor mass effect and peripheral nerve compression/involvement produce motor dysfunction and muscle weakness.

edges/12.description: Sequential CDKN2A and PRC2 loss in a plexiform neurofibroma drives transformation to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

evidence.snippet: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant genetic disease and one of the most common inherited tumor predisposition syndromes, affecting 1 in 3000 individuals worldwide.
evidence.explanation: Establishes NF1 as the autosomal dominant tumor predisposition gene underlying neurofibroma formation.

genes/0.notes: Germline loss-of-function NF1 variants (autosomal dominant; ~50% de novo) predispose to neurofibromas, which form after a somatic second hit inactivates the remaining allele. NF1 encodes neurofibromin, a RAS-GAP tumor suppressor; over 3,000 pathogenic variants are documented, mostly truncating.

evidence.snippet: A total of 35 patients (70%) had a confirmed partial response as of March 29, 2019, and 28 of these patients had a durable response (lasting ≥1 year).
evidence.explanation: SPRINT phase 2 trial result establishing selumetinib efficacy in inoperable plexiform neurofibromas.

treatments/0.description: Oral MEK1/2 inhibitor that suppresses the RAF-MEK-ERK signaling driven by NF1 loss. FDA-approved (2020) for pediatric patients with symptomatic, inoperable NF1-associated plexiform neurofibromas; the pivotal phase 2 SPRINT trial showed durable partial responses with pain and quality-of-life benefit.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Selumetinib inhibits MEK1/2, blocking the constitutively active RAF-MEK-ERK cascade downstream of NF1 loss.

evidence.snippet: Recent advancements in targeted therapies, particularly MEK inhibitors, have introduced promising treatment options for patients with severe manifestations of NF1.
evidence.explanation: Review supporting MEK inhibitors as a class as targeted therapy for severe NF1 manifestations including plexiform neurofibromas.

treatments/1.description: Oral MEK inhibitor for NF1-associated symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas, with reported partial responses and improvements in pain and function; acneiform rash is a common class toxicity.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Mirdametinib inhibits MEK, blocking the constitutively active RAF-MEK-ERK cascade downstream of NF1 loss.

evidence.snippet: Surgical intervention is often limited by factors such as the inaccessibility of the tumor location, involvement of critical tissues, suboptimal timing, or the inability to achieve complete resection.
evidence.explanation: Describes the central limitations of surgical resection for neurofibromas, motivating medical (MEK inhibitor) therapy.

treatments/2.description: Operative removal or debulking of symptomatic neurofibromas; the only potentially curative local option, but many plexiform neurofibromas are unresectable and regrowth is common.

evidence.snippet: PPT1 catalyzes depalmitoylation of S-palmitoylated proteins for degradation and clearance by lysosomal hydrolases.
evidence.explanation: This establishes the upstream lysosomal enzymatic function lost in CLN1.

evidence.snippet: CLN1 is characterized by the accumulation of autofluorescent lysosomal storage material (AFSM) in neurons and robust neuroinflammation.
evidence.explanation: This supports lysosomal storage accumulation and neuroinflammation as core CLN1 pathobiology.

steps/1.description: PPT1 deficiency prevents normal depalmitoylation and lysosomal clearance of S-palmitoylated proteins. This produces autofluorescent storage material in neurons and disrupts lysosomal nutrient sensing, mTORC1/autophagy control, cholesterol trafficking, synaptic protein trafficking, and inflammatory glial signaling.

evidence.snippet: Despite this defect, mTORC1 was hyperactivated via the IGF1/PI3K/Akt-signaling pathway, which suppressed autophagy contributing to neuropathology.
evidence.explanation: The study supports a downstream CLN1 mechanism in which mTORC1 activation suppresses autophagy and worsens neuropathology.

steps/2.description: PPT1 loss disrupts lysosomal nutrient sensing and hyperactivates mTORC1 through IGF1/PI3K/Akt signaling, suppressing autophagy and contributing to neurologic injury.

evidence.snippet: In Cln1-/- mice, Ppt1 deficiency misroutes NPC1-dysregulating lysosomal cholesterol homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: This establishes a distinct cholesterol trafficking branch downstream of PPT1 deficiency.

steps/3.description: Persistent NPC1 palmitoylation and misrouting in PPT1 deficiency impair lysosomal cholesterol homeostasis, producing cholesterol-dependent mTORC1 activation, autophagy inhibition, and neuronal injury.

evidence.snippet: the absence of depalmitoylation stifles synaptic protein trafficking and contributes to neuroinflammation via an Akap5-associated mechanism.
evidence.explanation: This defines the AKAP5/NFAT synaptic-neuroinflammatory branch as a top-level downstream mechanism in CLN1.

steps/4.description: PPT1 deficiency causes excess AKAP5 palmitoylation at synapses, aberrant GluA1 synaptic scaling, NFAT sensitization, and increased neuroinflammatory signaling.

evidence.snippet: Despite this defect, mTORC1 was hyperactivated via the IGF1/PI3K/Akt-signaling pathway, which suppressed autophagy contributing to neuropathology.
evidence.explanation: This mouse and patient-cell study links PPT1 loss to mTORC1 activation, autophagy suppression, and neuropathology.

edges/1.description: PPT1 loss disrupts lysosomal nutrient sensing and activates mTORC1, suppressing autophagy and contributing to neurodegeneration.

evidence.snippet: In Cln1-/- mice, Ppt1 deficiency misroutes NPC1-dysregulating lysosomal cholesterol homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: This supports a CLN1-specific lysosomal cholesterol trafficking branch.

edges/2.description: PPT1 deficiency misroutes NPC1, leading to lysosomal cholesterol dysregulation, mTORC1 activation, autophagy inhibition, and neuronal injury in CLN1 model systems.

evidence.snippet: (NFAT), was sensitized in Ppt1-/- cortical neurons.
evidence.explanation: This CLN1 mouse-model study directly connects PPT1 loss with AKAP5, synaptic protein trafficking, NFAT signaling, and neuroinflammation.

edges/3.description: Excessive AKAP5 palmitoylation at Ppt1-deficient synapses sensitizes NFAT signaling and links synaptic trafficking defects to neuroinflammation.

evidence.snippet: This disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CLN1 gene, encoding palmitoyl-protein thioesterase-1 (PPT1).
evidence.explanation: This CLN1 mechanism paper directly links CLN1/PPT1 loss of function to CLN1 disease.

genes/0.notes: PPT1 encodes palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1, a lysosomal thioesterase that removes palmitate from S-palmitoylated proteins. Biallelic loss-of-function variants define the CLN1 enzyme-deficiency branch of NCL.

evidence.snippet: transplantation of HSPCs over-expressing hPPT1 by lentiviral gene transfer enhances the therapeutic benefit of HSPCs transplant
evidence.explanation: Mouse-model data support PPT1-restoring HSPC gene therapy as a disease-targeted experimental CLN1 strategy.

treatments/0.description: Lentiviral hPPT1-overexpressing HSPC therapy is a preclinical, disease-targeted strategy for CLN1. It is not established clinical care, but it supports the biological plausibility of PPT1 restoration.

evidence.snippet: All 12 ROBO1 variants reported in our study were single-nucleotide substitutions: 2 canonical splice site variants, 8 truncating variants, and 2 missense variants, the latter 2 located within the functionally important Ig and FN3 protein domains
evidence.explanation: The complete allelic spectrum and the domain localisation of the missense alleles.

evidence.snippet: The extracellular portion, responsible for homodimerization and Slit-ligand binding, contains 5 well-defined N-terminal Ig-like domains followed by 3 fibronectin type III (FN3) domains.
evidence.explanation: Establishes what the domains hit by the missense alleles actually do, which is why their location is the argument for pathogenicity.

evidence.snippet: indicating nonsense-mediated RNA decay of the truncating allele and exclusive expression of the missense allele
evidence.explanation: Transcript-level demonstration that a truncating allele is degraded, so the surviving hypomorphic allele sets the phenotype. This is the observation the dosage model is built on.

steps/1.description: Twelve variants across the cohort, all single-nucleotide substitutions: eight truncating, two canonical splice-site, and two missense. The two missense alleles land in the functionally important extracellular domains - one on a surface loop of the third immunoglobulin domain near the homodimerisation linker, the other on the second fibronectin type III domain - which is where SLIT binding and receptor dimerisation happen. All but one allele were absent from population and clinical variant databases.

evidence.snippet: Roundabout guidance receptors (ROBOs) constitute a highly conserved subfamily of immunoglobulin superfamily proteins characterized by a single-pass transmembrane domain and interaction with the soluble extracellular Slit ligands.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the receptor-ligand relationship this node is about.

evidence.snippet: ROBO1 was shown to both homodimerize and heterodimerize with ROBO2
evidence.explanation: Records the dimerisation partnerships, which matter because one missense allele sits next to the homodimerisation linker.

evidence.snippet: Ciliary morphology and abundance, however, was overall unaffected on staining with acetylated tubulin in immunofluorescent microscopy
evidence.explanation: A tested and negative ciliopathy hypothesis. Regraded from REFUTE to NO_EVIDENCE on review: the result does not contradict this node's claim that SLIT-ROBO guidance signalling is reduced - it bears on a different proposition, that the phenotype is ciliary, and finds nothing. It is kept here because a phenotype that resembles a ciliopathy without being one is exactly the kind of claim that needs its negative on the record.

steps/2.description:
ROBO1 is a 180 kDa single-pass receptor for the secreted SLIT ligands, conserved since its identification in a Drosophila screen for axon guidance mutants. It homodimerises, heterodimerises with ROBO2, and binds SLIT1/2/3 and the SRGAP adaptors; reducing it therefore reduces a repulsive positional signal rather than a growth or survival signal. Its paralogue ROBO2 and its ligand SLIT2 are already implicated in human CAKUT, which is the pathway-level context that made ROBO1 a credible candidate long before this cohort existed.
The cystic-kidney and multi-organ pattern raises a ciliopathy hypothesis, and this node records that it was tested and not supported: ciliary morphology and abundance were normal in mutant collecting ducts and ureteric bud tips.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry of endogenous ROBO1 in fetal control kidneys dating from 14 and 21 WG showed ROBO1 localization at the outer nephrogenic zone within comma-shaped bodies and S-shaped bodies supporting a role of ROBO1 in normal nephrogenesis
evidence.explanation: Puts the protein in the right human tissue at the right developmental stage. This is human, not model-organism, expression data, which is what makes it the strongest single piece of mechanism in the entry.

evidence.snippet: the subcortical nephrogenic zone presented abolished in renal tissue from ID 8 at 22 WG accompanied by an absence of ROBO1 staining in severely dysplastic and cystic renal parenchyma
evidence.explanation: The matched patient tissue: no ROBO1 staining, no nephrogenic zone, dysplastic kidney. Expression and loss in the same experiment.

steps/3.description: ROBO1 protein sits in the human fetal kidney precisely where nephrons are being made - the outer nephrogenic zone, in comma-shaped and S-shaped bodies - at 14 and 21 weeks of gestation. In a 22-week fetus carrying biallelic ROBO1 variants that zone was gone and the staining with it, leaving dysplastic cystic parenchyma. Because the ureteric bud's position along the nephric duct determines whether a kidney forms at all and whether the ureter inserts correctly, a guidance failure at this step produces the whole clinical range at once: agenesis where the bud never emerges, reflux and junction obstruction where it emerges in the wrong place, dysplasia where branching miscarries.

evidence.snippet: ROBO1, which was originally identified in a Drosophila mutant screen, was shown to be crucial for proper axon guidance and neocortical development.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the receptor's canonical neural function, which is what the CNS phenotype is proposed to follow from.

evidence.snippet: His neurodevelopmental phenotype was also striking for the observation of mirror hand movement disorder. No likely damaging variants in DCC or RAD51, previously associated with autosomal dominant mirror movements
evidence.explanation: The mirror-movement observation with the two competing genes excluded. This is the closest thing in the cohort to a direct clinical test of a midline-crossing defect.

evidence.snippet: partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, absence of pyramidal tracts, and dentate nuclei hypoplasia
evidence.explanation: Fetal neuropathology showing absent pyramidal tracts alongside the callosal defect - two crossing systems failing together.

steps/4.description: ROBO1 was identified as an axon guidance receptor and is required for neocortical development. The neurological phenotype in this cohort is correspondingly midline-weighted: corpus callosum thinning or partial or splenial agenesis, absent pyramidal tracts in all three fetuses, ventriculomegaly, cerebellar vermis and dentate nucleus hypoplasia, and brainstem hypoplasia. One patient had mirror movements without a variant in DCC or RAD51, the two established mirror-movement genes - which is a direct clinical readout of failed decussation, since mirror movements arise when corticospinal projections that should cross do not.

evidence.snippet: Regarding pituitary malformations, we also observed variable expressivity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes pituitary malformation as part of the biallelic phenotype and states that its expressivity varies, which is what this node claims.

evidence.snippet: The roundabout receptor-1 gene (ROBO1) plays critical roles in axonal guidance and cell migration. Recently, mutations in the ROBO1 gene have been reported patients with PSIS.
evidence.explanation: Connects the gene's guidance function to stalk interruption specifically. INDIRECT: the reported patients are heterozygous, so this supports the developmental step rather than the recessive syndrome.

steps/5.description: The endocrine branch. The pituitary stalk is a midline structure whose formation depends on the same guidance signalling as the commissures, and ROBO1 was implicated in pituitary stalk interruption syndrome by heterozygous variants before this recessive entity was described. In the biallelic cohort the readout ranges from a missing posterior pituitary bright spot with no endocrine consequence, through hypopituitarism with hypogonadism and micropenis and reduced growth, to combined pituitary hormone deficiency with central diabetes insipidus in the heterozygous PSIS literature. Expressivity is explicitly variable, so this node describes a susceptible developmental step rather than an obligate lesion.

evidence.snippet: we examined Robo1 and 2 mutant mice and found that Robos regulate the correct targeting of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) axons along the entire visual projection.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the receptor family's role in visual pathway targeting. INDIRECT and MODEL_ORGANISM: mouse, and not in a disease model.

evidence.snippet: The optic chiasm was expanded along the rostro-caudal axis
evidence.explanation: The specific midline defect - an expanded optic chiasm with ectopic crossing points - which is the visual-pathway counterpart of the commissural phenotype this entry curates elsewhere.

evidence.snippet: These defects were more pronounced in Robo2 than Robo1 knockout animals, implicating Robo2 as the predominant Robo receptor in visual system development.
evidence.explanation: The caveat that keeps this node a proposal. If Robo2 is the predominant receptor in visual development, ROBO1 loss alone is a weaker explanation for the ocular phenotype than for the renal or commissural ones, and the entry should not imply otherwise.

steps/6.description:
The ocular branch - the "oculo" of the disease name, which the entry previously described in phenotypes without modelling. ROBO receptors target retinal ganglion cell axons along the whole visual projection, and in Robo mutant mice the optic chiasm is expanded with ectopic crossing points and axons projecting where they should not. That is the same midline-crossing decision the commissural branch of this entry describes, applied to the visual pathway, and it is the most plausible route from ROBO1 loss to the strabismus reported across this cohort.
Stated carefully: the mouse work is on Robo1 and Robo2 mutants and finds Robo2 the predominant receptor in visual development, so this node is a mechanism proposal for the human ocular phenotype rather than a demonstrated one. No human ocular pathology has been reported in this syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Kidney and genitourinary manifestation included unilateral or bilateral kidney agenesis, vesicoureteral junction obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, posterior urethral valve, genital malformation, and increased kidney echogenicity.
evidence.explanation: The full renal and genitourinary spectrum of the cohort, in one place.

evidence.snippet: renal function stabilized over the years until a slowly progressive decrease in function led to bilateral atrophic kidneys and end-stage kidney disease at the age of 44
evidence.explanation: The adult end of the range, and the reason this diagnosis belongs in the workup of unexplained adult chronic kidney failure.

steps/7.description: The defining organ phenotype and the one with prognostic weight. Its range within nine people is the whole CAKUT spectrum - bilateral agenesis with Potter sequence at the lethal end, unilateral agenesis and reflux nephropathy in the middle, increased echogenicity with mildly reduced kidney size at the mild end. The index patient reached end-stage kidney disease at 44, so this is a phenotype that can present in adulthood as unexplained chronic kidney failure with the congenital origin overlooked.

evidence.snippet: Further clinical characteristics were remarkably heterogeneous, including neurodevelopmental defects, intellectual impairment, cerebral malformations, eye anomalies, and cardiac defects.
evidence.explanation: Names the extrarenal domains and, importantly, states that they are heterogeneous rather than obligate.

evidence.snippet: Motor and cognitive skills developed normally.
evidence.explanation: The index patient's normal cognition, which contradicts neurodevelopmental impairment being an obligate feature. Recorded as REFUTE against that stronger reading rather than dropped.

steps/8.description: Clinically: intellectual impairment and psychomotor delay in most, dysmorphic facial features in eight of nine, and structural midline findings on imaging. Notably not universal - the adult index patient's motor and cognitive development was normal and his only MRI finding was a missing posterior pituitary bright spot, so a normal neurodevelopmental history does not exclude the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: eye anomalies (bilateral strabismus, atrophic iris), and dextrocardia were part of the clinical syndrome
evidence.explanation: Documents the ocular findings as part of the syndrome, with the iris anomaly alongside.

steps/9.description: The most consistent eye finding, present in at least three patients, bilateral. Reported alongside an atrophic iris in one. Strabismus in a guidance-receptor disorder is worth taking seriously as a possible connectivity phenotype rather than a coincidental refractive one, though the cohort does not establish that.

edges/1.description: Loss of receptor available to bind SLIT ligand at the cell surface.

edges/2.description: Loss of the positional signal that places and branches the ureteric bud.

edges/3.description: Loss of the repulsive signal that governs midline crossing.

edges/4.description: Loss of the same guidance signal at the midline structure that becomes the pituitary stalk.

edges/5.description: Loss of ROBO-mediated targeting of retinal ganglion cell axons through the optic chiasm.

edges/6.description: The clinical renal phenotype produced by the guidance failure.

edges/7.description: The clinical CNS phenotype.

edges/8.description: Stalk and hypothalamic-pituitary involvement is part of the same midline malformation spectrum.

edges/9.description: Proposed route from mistargeted visual projections to the ocular phenotype; not demonstrated in human tissue.

evidence.snippet: we here propose biallelic ROBO1 variants as causing syndromic, but viable CAKUT phenotypes in humans
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assertion, with the authors' own emphasis that biallelic loss is compatible with life - which had been the open question.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to our observations in ROBO1, VUR associated with ROBO2 was observed on monoallelic variation and dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes this gene's inheritance pattern from its paralogue's, which is what keeps the two entities separate.

genes/0.notes: The sole gene for this disorder, at 3p12.3, encoding the 180 kDa roundabout guidance receptor 1. Biallelic variants cause this recessive syndrome; monoallelic variants have separately been reported in congenital heart disease and in pituitary stalk interruption syndrome, and the unaffected status of the carrier parents here is the evidence that those are a different, lower-penetrance situation rather than the same disease in milder form. The paralogue ROBO2 and the ligand SLIT2 are independently implicated in CAKUT, but by monoallelic variants with incomplete penetrance, which is the contrast that makes ROBO1's recessive pattern notable.

evidence.snippet: The 44-year-old index patient (ID 1) was genetically evaluated for chronic kidney failure of unknown etiology while awaiting kidney transplantation.
evidence.explanation: Documents that a patient with this genotype reached transplant candidacy. INDIRECT: the source reports the clinical situation, not an outcome of transplantation in this disease.

treatments/0.description: The end of the renal course for the severe survivors, and the reason this diagnosis has prognostic weight rather than only explanatory value. The index patient reached end-stage kidney disease at 44 and was on the transplant waiting list when the genotype was found. Nothing modifies the underlying malformation; this treats its consequence.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces failed renal function. It does not act on the developmental lesion, which is complete before birth.

evidence.snippet: he suffered from repetitive pyelonephritis due to VUR caused by unilateral ureterovesical junction obstruction and a posterior urethral valve requiring surgical intervention within his first year of life
evidence.explanation: Documents the surgical intervention and the lesions it addressed. INDIRECT: one patient, and the subsequent stability is not attributed to the surgery by the source.

treatments/1.description: Where the ureteric-bud lesion produces obstruction rather than agenesis, the consequence is recurrent pyelonephritis and progressive scarring, and it is surgically addressable. The index patient had a posterior urethral valve and ureterovesical junction obstruction corrected in his first year; his renal function then stayed stable for four decades. That sequence is an argument for early urological assessment, though a single course is not evidence of benefit.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Relieves obstruction and reflux, addressing the secondary injury rather than the malformation.

evidence.snippet: We conclude and emphasize that ROBO1 should be investigated in patients with PSIS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ROBO1 as a cause of the pituitary phenotype that this treatment addresses. INDIRECT twice over: the patient is heterozygous rather than biallelic, and the source recommends genetic testing rather than reporting a treatment outcome.

treatments/2.description: Where the pituitary is involved, the deficiencies are replaceable, which makes this the one part of the syndrome with a treatment that restores function rather than managing damage. Reported in the ROBO1-related pituitary literature rather than in the NORS cohort itself, so the link from this entity to this treatment runs through the shared gene.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Replaces the hormone output lost when the midline pituitary structures fail to form. It does not act on the malformation itself.

evidence.snippet: in patients with already established ROBO1-associated cardiac or neuronal disorders, screening for kidney involvement is indicated.
evidence.explanation: The cross-organ screening recommendation that a molecular diagnosis enables. INDIRECT: it is a diagnostic recommendation being used to support a counselling and surveillance role.

evidence.snippet: Lastly, we describe a previously unreported family with 3 affected fetal cases
evidence.explanation: The recurrence this counselling addresses: three affected pregnancies in one family. INDIRECT: it documents the recurrence, not the effect of counselling on it.

treatments/3.description:
A recessive syndrome with a one-in-four recurrence risk and, at the severe end, a lethal prenatal phenotype - so counselling with prenatal or preimplantation options is a substantive part of care after a first affected pregnancy. Three of the nine reported individuals are fetuses from one family, which is what that risk looks like in practice.
The counselling has a second, less obvious use. Two patients in this cohort were found by re-examining the kidneys of people already carrying a ROBO1-related cardiac or neurological diagnosis, so a molecular diagnosis in one organ system should prompt screening of the others.

hypotheses/0.description: Biallelic reduction of ROBO1 below a threshold impairs SLIT-ROBO signalling in every tissue that uses it to position structures during development. The three affected organ systems are the three places where that requirement is strictest and least redundant: commissural and pyramidal axon guidance across the CNS midline, ureteric bud outgrowth and branching in the nephrogenic zone, and ocular development. Whether an individual is severely or mildly affected is set by which pair of alleles they carry, not by which tissue is involved - the same genotype affects all three. CANONICAL because the receptor biology, the human fetal kidney expression, the mouse renal and cardiac phenotypes, and the human genetics all point the same way.

evidence.snippet: variability of the kidney disease suggests gene dosage effects due to a combination of null alleles with mild hypomorphic alleles
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of the hypothesis, offered as a suggestion rather than a demonstration.

open_questions/0.rationale: The authors propose exactly this and the cohort is consistent with it: the index patient survived to 44 with a truncating allele undergoing nonsense-mediated decay in trans with a missense allele that gnomAD lists at 0.04% in Europeans, while the fetal cases carried two frameshifts. But nine individuals cannot establish a genotype-phenotype rule, the ascertainment differs between the fetal and living arms, and no functional assay quantifies residual signalling for any allele. This is the question with the most immediate clinical consequence in the entry - it is what prenatal counselling for a newly identified biallelic genotype would turn on - so recording it as unresolved matters more than usual.

evidence.snippet: The virus enters the host cells through Ephrin B2/B3 receptors
evidence.explanation: States the receptor pair mediating Nipah virus entry into host cells.

evidence.snippet: inherent ability to use the evolutionarily conserved and widely expressed cellular receptor Ephrin B2 for entry
evidence.explanation: Establishes that ephrin-B2 is conserved and widely expressed, which is what makes receptor distribution determine tropism.

evidence.snippet: Henipavirus entry is initiated by the attachment of the G envelope glycoprotein to host cell membrane receptors.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the viral attachment glycoprotein G engaging host cell receptors as the initiating step of henipavirus entry.

steps/0.description: The Nipah virus attachment glycoprotein engages the host ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 receptors to mediate entry into host cells. Because ephrin-B2 is evolutionarily conserved and widely expressed on vascular endothelium, and ephrin-B3 on neurons, the tissue distribution of these receptors is what determines the endothelial and neuronal tropism that drives the rest of the disease, and also underlies the virus's broad host-species range.

evidence.snippet: Similar to other paramyxoviruses, Henipaviruses inhibit IFN signal transduction through a virus-encoded protein called V.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the V protein as the henipavirus-encoded inhibitor of interferon signal transduction.

evidence.snippet: This sequestration of STAT1 and STAT2 prevents STAT activation and blocks antiviral IFN signaling.
evidence.explanation: States the molecular consequence - STAT1/STAT2 sequestration prevents STAT activation and blocks antiviral interferon signaling.

evidence.snippet: we show here that NiV can inhibit IFN-dependent antiviral signaling via a NiV P-dependent sequestration of STAT1 and STAT2 into viral IBs
evidence.explanation: Adds the phosphoprotein P arm, sequestering STAT1/STAT2 into viral inclusion bodies, alongside the V-protein mechanism.

evidence.snippet: the pathogenic potential of NiV is linked to its ability to block antiviral responses
evidence.explanation: Links interferon antagonism directly to the pathogenic potential of the virus, which is why this node sits upstream of dissemination.

steps/1.description: Nipah virus accessory proteins expressed from the P gene antagonize type I interferon signaling by binding and sequestering STAT1 and STAT2. The V protein induces cytoplasmic high-molecular-weight STAT-containing complexes, and the phosphoprotein P sequesters STAT1/STAT2 into viral inclusion bodies; both prevent STAT activation and nuclear translocation. Blocking the innate antiviral response is what permits the virus to disseminate systemically before an effective interferon response is mounted.

evidence.snippet: The underlying pathology seen in the ferret closely resembles that seen in Nipah virus infected humans, characterized as a widespread multisystemic vasculitis, with virus replicating in highly vascular tissues including lung, spleen and brain, with recoverable virus from a variety of tissues.
evidence.explanation:
Documents systemic dissemination with virus recoverable from multiple
tissues. MODEL_ORGANISM because the observation is in the ferret model,
though the authors state the pathology closely resembles human disease.

steps/2.description: Unrestrained by the interferon response, the virus replicates in and spreads through highly vascular tissues, producing a widespread multisystemic vasculitis and the non-specific systemic febrile prodrome - fever, headache and vomiting - that precedes organ-specific disease.

evidence.snippet: The main histopathological findings included a systemic vasculitis with extensive thrombosis and parenchymal necrosis, particularly in the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy findings from human cases show systemic vasculitis with thrombosis and necrosis.

evidence.snippet: IHC analysis showed widespread presence of Nipah virus antigens in endothelial and smooth muscle cells of blood vessels.
evidence.explanation: Immunohistochemistry localizes Nipah antigen to vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells.

steps/3.description: Nipah virus infects vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, producing a systemic vasculitis with thrombosis and parenchymal necrosis, especially in the central nervous system.

evidence.snippet: Endothelial cell damage, necrosis, and syncytial giant cell formation were seen in affected vessels.
evidence.explanation: Syncytial giant cells are observed in affected vessels of human autopsy tissue.

steps/4.description: Nipah virus induces fusion of infected cells into multinucleated syncytial giant cells, prominent in affected blood vessels.

evidence.snippet: Abundant viral antigens were also seen in various parenchymal cells, particularly in neurons.
evidence.explanation: Viral antigen is abundant in neurons, evidencing direct CNS neuronal infection.

evidence.snippet: Human infection manifests as a rapidly progressive encephalitis accounting for extremely high mortality rates.
evidence.explanation: The review characterizes human Nipah infection as a rapidly progressive encephalitis.

steps/5.description: The virus infects neurons of the central nervous system, producing an acute encephalitis alongside vasculitis-associated injury.

evidence.snippet: Nipah virus infection produced rapidly progressive severe illness affecting the central nervous and respiratory systems.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the respiratory system, alongside the CNS, as a primary target of the infection.

evidence.snippet: including a severe respiratory component, appear distinct from clinical characteristics reported during earlier outbreaks in other countries.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the severe respiratory component as what distinguishes Bangladesh disease from the earlier Malaysian outbreak.

evidence.snippet: whereas many patients infected with NiV clade I had added severe pulmonary involvement
evidence.explanation: Attributes severe pulmonary involvement specifically to clade I infection.

evidence.snippet: NiV clade II isolated cases led to a pure encephalitic syndrome (neurological symptoms without respiratory manifestations)
evidence.explanation: The contrasting clade II picture, without respiratory manifestations, establishes that the pulmonary arm is clade-dependent.

evidence.snippet: Outbreaks of HeV and NiV have led to severe respiratory disease and encephalitis in humans and animals characterized by a high mortality rate.
evidence.explanation: Corroborates severe respiratory disease as a core outcome of henipavirus outbreaks alongside encephalitis.

steps/6.description: Beyond the encephalitic arm, Nipah virus produces severe pulmonary involvement with respiratory tract infection and vascular injury of the lungs.
